claims.text: CrFeCoNiX alloys can form a protective, slow-growing oxide layer that persists above 900 °C when their composition minimizes interfacial misfit dislocations and defect-induced stresses.
Optimizing Al content minimizes interfacial misfit dislocations and defect-induced stresses.
Enhanced metal/oxide bonding promotes in situ formation of a coherent alumina-like scale.
The proposed initial material is a single-phase metallic solid solution of CrFeCoNiX, where X is Si, Mn, or Al.
DFT and kinetic Monte Carlo can quantify defect formation energies and interfacial bonding strength as reactive-element composition is varied.
High-temperature XRD and electron microscopy can validate the predicted interfacial and oxidation behavior.
The proposed exposure is 900–950 °C for 100–500 hours in oxygen-rich or mildly corrosive atmospheres under controlled oxygen partial pressure.
Reactive-element content, especially Al, modulates metal/oxide interfacial coherence and defect density.
Metal/oxide interfacial coherence and defect density govern formation and stability of the protective oxide scale.
An optimal Al content produces stronger interfacial metal–oxide bonding.
Stronger interfacial bonding minimizes misfit dislocations and defect-induced stresses.
Reduced misfit dislocations and defect-induced stresses promote a coherent, slow-growing, alumina-dominated scale.
Lower or otherwise non-optimal Al content produces more interfacial defects and thereby accelerates oxide growth, cracking, and spallation.
Substitution with Si or Mn does not provide bonding characteristics comparable to optimized Al.
Alloys with higher Al content will have significantly lower defect formation energies and reduced interfacial strain.
Higher-Al alloys will form thinner, more uniform, and more adherent oxide scales with less cracking and spallation than lower-Al, Si-containing, or Mn-containing comparators.
The baseline consists of lower-Al CrFeCoNiX alloys or Si/Mn variants tested under oxidation conditions identical to those used for the higher-Al alloys.
The hypothesis is limited to single-phase solid solutions or selected carefully controlled multiphase states exposed at temperatures of at least 900 °C under defined oxygen partial pressures.
The results may not apply at substantially different temperatures or in unanticipated corrosive regimes.
Failure of lower predicted defect energies or increased Al content to correlate with improved scale coherence and adherence under identical conditions would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: X is defined as one of Si, Mn, or Al, but the intervention and baseline propose varying Al content across CrFeCoNiX alloys. Adding Al to an X = Si or Mn alloy creates a different multicomponent system unless Al replaces X; that compositional operation is not specified.
The mechanism predicts an optimum, potentially non-monotonic Al content, whereas the predicted outcome states that higher Al content is better, implying a monotonic trend.

Lower defect formation energies are predicted to accompany fewer interfacial defects, but lower formation energy commonly makes a specified defect easier to form. The relevant defect species and sign convention are not defined, leaving the prediction internally ambiguous.

The initial state is restricted to a single-phase solid solution, while the boundary also admits selected multiphase states without defining which states qualify or how phase constitution is controlled.
